facts.statement: The genus Osteodontornis was described by Howard in 1957.
facts.quote: parent_authority: Howard, 1957

facts.statement: Fossils of Osteodontornis date to the Miocene epoch.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Miocene (but see text)

facts.statement: Osteodontornis is an extinct genus of seabirds.
facts.quote: Osteodontornis is an extinct seabird genus.

facts.statement: The genus Osteodontornis contains only one named species, Osteodontornis orri.
facts.quote: It contains a single named species, Osteodontornis orri

facts.statement: The species O. orri was named in honor of paleontologist Phil C. Orr.
facts.quote: O. orri was named after Santa Barbara Museum of Natural History paleontologist Phil C. Orr

facts.statement: Osteodontornis is classified in the order Odontopterygiformes, with uncertain close relatives including pelicans, storks, or waterfowl.
facts.quote: they seem to be rather close relatives of either pelicans and storks, or of waterfowl, and are here placed in the order Odontopterygiformes

facts.statement: It is debated whether Osteodontornis is a junior synonym of the genus Cyphornis.
facts.quote: It may be that Osteodontornis is a junior synonym of Cyphornis.

facts.statement: Osteodontornis orri had a wingspan of 5.5 to 6 meters and stood 1.2 meters tall on the ground.
facts.quote: With a wingspan of 5.5 to 6 m and a height of 1.2 m when on the ground

facts.statement: The beak comprised about three-quarters of the head length and featured hollow or cancellous bone-filled tooth-like serrations.
facts.quote: Its beak made up about three-quarters of the head's length and had bony tooth-like serrations that were hollow or maybe filled with cancellous bone.

facts.statement: Due to its heavy beak, O. orri likely held its bill between its shoulders during flight, similar to modern pelicans.
facts.quote: The beak was so heavy the creature probably held it between its shoulders while in flight, just like modern pelicans do.

facts.statement: O. orri was a seabird that primarily fed on squid and other soft-bodied prey.
facts.quote: It was a seabird that apparently lived mainly off squid and other soft-bodied prey

facts.statement: The downward-pointing beak serrations were adapted for grabbing slippery pelagic animals like cephalopods, likely snatched from the water during flight or swimming.
facts.quote: The downward-pointing "teeth" were ideal for digging into and holding slippery, soft-skinned pelagic animals such as cephalopods that were probably snatched out of the water in flight or while swimming.

facts.statement: Despite its light build, O. orri was likely unable to dive effectively.
facts.quote: Lightly built as it was, O. orri was probably not a good diver and may have found it impossible to dive at all.

facts.statement: O. orri likely nested on high plateaus to facilitate takeoff by walking into the wind.
facts.quote: It probably built its nest on high plateaus or similar places, where it could easily take flight by simply walking into the wind with wings spread.

facts.statement: The type specimen of Osteodontornis orri was found in Late Miocene shale in California and includes bone pieces and feather impressions.
facts.quote: The type specimen of O. orri, SBMNH 309, is a rather comprehensive fossil preserved mostly as imprint, with some bone pieces and even feather impressions in addition; it was found in Clarendonian (Late Miocene) shale of California (USA).

facts.statement: Osteodontornis fossils are generally from the Miocene and are often fragmented because the bird had thin and tender bones.
facts.quote: This species is well documented from various locations of generally Miocene age, although usually by much fragmented remains due to the thin and tender bones it had.

facts.statement: Fossils of Osteodontornis have been found on both sides of the North Pacific.
facts.quote: Most importantly, it was found on both sides of the North Pacific.

facts.statement: Fossils from Venezuela and Peru might belong to a distinct genus rather than Osteodontornis, and their connection to Atlantic Pelagornis cannot be ruled out because the Isthmus of Panama had not formed yet.
facts.quote: Similar fossils have been found in the Middle Miocene Capadare Formation of Venezuela and from the Late Miocene of the Pisco Formation of Peru; they might rather be of a distinct but closely related genus, and it must be remembered that at that their time the Isthmus of Panama had not been formed yet so that an affiliation with the Atlantic Pelagornis cannot be discounted.

facts.statement: A premaxilla tip from Venezuela suggests that the animal could have had a wingspan exceeding 7 meters.
facts.quote: The former, specimen MBLUZ-P-5093 from Cueva del Zumbador in Falcón State, is a premaxilla tip of immense dimensions; its bearer might have exceeded a wingspan of 7 m in life.

facts.statement: Recent authors divide Neogene pseudotooth birds by geography (Atlantic to Pelagornis, North Pacific to Osteodontornis), but this division remains a hypothesis pending more well-preserved material.
facts.quote: Generally, recent authors have tended to place large Neogene pseudotooth bird fossils from the Atlantic in Pelagornis, and those from the North Pacific in Osteodontornis. It remains to be seen if this east–west division can be upheld, but biogeographically it seems quite sensible at least as a working hypothesis until sufficient well-preserved material has been found to make an in-depth study.

facts.statement: Osteodontornis belongs to the parent group Pelagornithidae.
facts.quote: Parent group: Pelagornithidae

facts.statement: Osteodontornis is classified in the family Pelagornithidae.
facts.quote: Family: Pelagornithidae

facts.statement: Osteodontornis lived from the Thanetian to the Messinian, between 59.24 and 5.333 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Thanetian to Messinian (59.24 to 5.333 million years ago)
